rw: Authority is the formally granted right to make decisions, give instructions and expect them to be followed, which comes with a managerial position in the organization's structure.

ww.Friendship with the coworkers on a team: Friendship is a social bond between peers and carries no formal right to give orders or make binding decisions for the organization.
ww.Popularity with the staff and with the c: Popularity may help a manager gain goodwill, but being liked by staff and customers does not give anyone the formal right to direct other people.
ww.Wealth and money held by a manager perso: Personal wealth is a private asset and gives no legitimate organizational right to decide or command, so money held by a manager is not authority.

rw: Authority is the formal right to decide and direct, while responsibility is the obligation to carry out assigned duties and answer for the results, so this pairing is accurate.

ww.Responsibility is the right to decide wh: This reverses the two terms. Responsibility is the obligation to perform assigned work, not the right to decide, and authority is the right to decide, not the duty to work.
ww.Authority is the duty to report, while r: Authority is not a duty to report, and responsibility is not a right to rest. Responsibility is an obligation to perform, so this definition removes the accountability it carries.
ww.They are identical and mean exactly the: The two terms are distinct. Authority is the right to decide and direct, while responsibility is the duty to perform and answer for results, so they are not identical.

rw: Tactical planning turns the broad strategy into specific departmental actions, usually over a shorter term such as one year, which bridges strategic goals and daily operations.

ww.Setting the mission statement that descr: Setting the mission statement that explains why a company exists is a top-level strategic task, not tactical planning, which works at the department level on a shorter time horizon.
ww.Choosing the company name and logo that: Choosing a company name and logo is a branding and marketing decision. It does not translate strategy into departmental actions, so it is not tactical planning.
ww.Daily task lists only, which workers use: Daily task lists describe operational planning at the worker level, not tactical planning. The word "only" also narrows it wrongly, since tactical plans cover whole departments and longer periods.

rw: An SOP is a documented set of steps for doing a routine task the same way every time, which keeps quality and safety consistent across staff.

ww.A one-time suggestion made by an employe: A one-time suggestion is an informal idea raised once, whereas an SOP is a standing written procedure that people follow repeatedly, so a single suggestion cannot be an SOP.
ww.A company slogan used in advertising and: A slogan is a marketing phrase used in advertising and on packaging, while an SOP is an internal instruction document. The two serve entirely different purposes.
ww.A pay scale that lists the wages for eac: A pay scale lists wages by job grade and belongs to compensation management. An SOP instead describes steps for performing a task, so this does not match.

rw: Kaizen is the Japanese philosophy of continuous small improvements made by all employees over time, which gradually raises quality and efficiency without needing large, disruptive changes.

ww.A budgeting tool used to plan yearly spe: A budgeting tool plans spending for a year, while kaizen is about improving work methods continuously. Kaizen is a philosophy of improvement, not a financial planning document.
ww.A one-time overhaul done by outside cons: Kaizen is not a one-time overhaul. Its core idea is steady, ongoing small changes by everyone, whereas a single consultant-led makeover is a big, one-off change.
ww.A legal term used in contracts and court: Kaizen is a Japanese management concept, not a legal term. Contracts and court filings use different vocabulary, so this has no connection to the word's real meaning.

rw: Six Sigma is a data-driven approach that measures processes to cut defects and variation, aiming for about 3.4 defects per million opportunities, which improves quality.

ww.A hiring plan that sets out how many wor: A hiring plan sets recruitment numbers and is an HR planning tool. Six Sigma is a quality method focused on reducing defects, so recruitment targets are unrelated to it.
ww.A sales method used to close deals with: A sales method closes deals with customers, but Six Sigma is a process-quality approach. It targets production and service defects, not selling techniques or deal closing.
ww.A logo style used in the branding of the: A logo style is a branding choice. Six Sigma is a statistical quality approach, so a visual identity has no link to it despite the sigma symbol.

rw: Lean management means eliminating waste such as extra steps, idle time and defects while still delivering value to customers, which improves efficiency without lowering what the customer receives.

ww.Delaying work until the very last minute: Lean management removes waste and does not mean delaying work. Putting tasks off until the deadline usually creates rushed output and idle time, which lean specifically tries to avoid.
ww.Cutting staff only, to lower the cost of: Lean is about waste removal while delivering value, not simply cutting staff. Layoffs alone can harm quality and morale, so a staff-cutting-only view misses the point.
ww.Making products slimmer and lighter to c: Lean refers to a management approach, not to making products physically slimmer or lighter. Product size and shipping weight are unrelated to waste elimination in processes.

rw: Benchmarking compares your performance and processes with best practices of leading organizations, which shows where gaps exist and how to improve, so this is the accurate definition.

ww.Copying products illegally from rivals a: Benchmarking is a legal, open comparison of practices and results. Copying rivals' products illegally is theft or infringement, which is a different and unlawful act.
ww.Building benches for parks and other pub: Building benches is a construction or public works activity. The word only sounds similar, and benchmarking is a management practice of measuring performance against others.
ww.Ignoring competitors and the market whil: Benchmarking requires looking closely at competitors and the market for best practices. Ignoring them and looking only inward is the opposite of comparing against leaders.

rw: Managers focus on processes, tasks and getting things done, while leaders inspire people and set direction. This captures the common distinction between the two roles accurately.

ww.Managers never lead and leaders never ma: The claim that managers never lead and leaders never manage is too absolute. Many people do both, and the roles overlap, so this statement is wrong.
ww.They are identical, since both roles do: The roles are not identical. Managers organize and control processes, and leaders inspire and set vision, so claiming they do exactly the same work ignores the real difference.
ww.Leaders only do paperwork and file repor: This reverses the roles. Inspiring people is the leader's focus, and paperwork and reports fit management tasks, and saying leaders only do paperwork is untrue.

rw: An autocratic leader makes decisions alone, with little or no input from the team, and expects staff to comply with the orders given.

ww.A leader who asks the team to vote on ea: A leader who has the team vote on each decision is democratic or participative, not autocratic, since an autocrat keeps decision power rather than sharing it.
ww.A leader who delegates everything to the: Delegating everything and staying away describes a laissez-faire leader. An autocratic leader stays in control and directs the work instead of stepping back.
ww.A leader who gives total freedom to the: Giving the team total freedom with no direction is laissez-faire. Autocratic leaders do the opposite by controlling decisions tightly, so this does not describe them.

rw: A democratic or participative leader involves team members in decisions by seeking their input and ideas, which builds ownership and commitment while the leader still guides the process.

ww.A leader who avoids decisions entirely: Avoiding decisions entirely is a failure to lead, not a democratic style. A democratic leader still makes decisions, but does so after gathering the team's views.
ww.A leader who gives no guidance at all to: Giving staff no guidance at all describes a hands-off or laissez-faire approach. A democratic leader still offers direction while inviting the team's input on decisions.
ww.A leader who decides alone, with no inpu: Deciding alone with no input is autocratic leadership, the opposite of democratic leadership, which is built on involving the team in the decision.

rw: The autocratic style lets one leader decide quickly and give clear orders without debate, which is often the most suitable approach when an immediate decision is required in an emergency.

ww.No leadership: Having no leadership in an emergency wastes scarce time and leaves people without direction, so it is the least appropriate response when an immediate decision is required.
ww.Democratic: Democratic decision making takes time for discussion and consensus, which an emergency does not allow. It suits calm situations rather than ones needing an immediate decision.
ww.Laissez-faire: Laissez-faire leaves decisions to the team with little direction, which risks confusion and delay when a fast, clear call is needed during an emergency.

rw: Laissez-faire leaders give a capable, skilled team freedom to choose its own methods, with little interference, which works well when members are experienced and self-motivated.

ww.Bureaucratic: Bureaucratic leadership relies on strict rules and procedures, which limits freedom. It does not describe a leader who lets a skilled team choose its own approach.
ww.Autocratic: An autocratic leader keeps decisions and control, which is the opposite of giving a skilled team freedom to select how it works.
ww.Charismatic only: Charismatic leadership relies on personal charm to inspire, not on handing over freedom. The word "only" also makes it too narrow to describe the hands-off approach given here.

rw: Charismatic leadership uses personal charm and the ability to inspire followers, who are drawn to the leader's vision and enthusiasm rather than to rules or rewards alone.

ww.Leading through paperwork and written or: Leading through paperwork and written orders describes a bureaucratic style. Charismatic leadership depends on personal charm and inspiration, which the question states directly, not on documents.
ww.Leading through rules and procedures wri: Leading through rules and procedures in manuals is bureaucratic leadership. Charismatic leaders rely on their personality and ability to inspire rather than on written rules.
ww.Leading through fear and punishments han: Leading through fear and punishment is coercive, not charismatic. Charismatic leaders attract followers through admiration and inspiration, not threats or penalties.

rw: Self-awareness, the ability to recognize your own emotions and their effect on others, is one of the core components of emotional intelligence alongside self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.

ww.Memorized facts: Memorized facts measure knowledge recall, not emotional intelligence, which concerns understanding and managing emotions in oneself and others rather than storing information.
ww.Speed typing: Speed typing is a technical skill with no link to recognizing or managing emotions, so it is not a component of emotional intelligence.
ww.Math skill: Math skill is a cognitive ability tied to analytical intelligence, not to emotional intelligence, which covers awareness and management of feelings and relationships.

rw: Integrity in leadership means being honest and keeping values and actions consistent, so people can trust the leader to do what is right and say what is true.

ww.Being popular with the staff and the cus: Being popular is about being liked, which can change with the situation. Integrity is about moral principles, so popularity does not define it.
ww.Being strict about rules and deadlines a: Being strict about rules and deadlines is discipline or rigidity. Integrity concerns honesty and moral consistency, which a strict person may or may not show.
ww.Being wealthy enough to pay for the need: Wealth has no bearing on integrity. A leader's honesty and values do not depend on money, so being wealthy enough to pay for the team's needs is irrelevant.

rw: Leading by example means modeling the behavior you expect from others, such as arriving on time and working hard, so your actions match your words and set the standard.

ww.Delegating all tasks while taking the cr: Delegating everything and taking credit is the opposite of leading by example, because it shows the leader sets a poor standard and avoids sharing recognition.
ww.Avoiding work while others do all of the: Avoiding work while others do all the tasks sets a bad example. Leading by example requires the leader to take part and show the expected effort.
ww.Giving orders only and never doing any t: Giving orders without doing any tasks is not modeling behavior. Leading by example requires doing the work yourself, so people see the standard in action.

rw: Vision in leadership is a clear picture of a desirable future that guides decisions and inspires people to work toward a shared goal.

ww.A yearly budget that lists the money the: A yearly budget lists planned spending and income, which is a financial plan. Vision in leadership is a picture of a desirable future, not a budget document.
ww.Good eyesight that helps a manager read: Good eyesight is a physical ability and has nothing to do with leadership vision, which is a figurative idea about the future, not about reading reports.
ww.A to-do list of tasks that employees sho: A weekly to-do list covers short-term tasks, whereas vision is a long-term picture of a desirable future that gives direction and inspiration beyond daily or weekly tasks.

rw: Power in organizations is the ability to influence the behavior of others, whether through position, expertise, rewards, coercion or personal appeal, so this is the correct definition.

ww.A budget set by the company each year: A budget is a financial plan for money, not power. Power in organizations is about the ability to influence people, not about yearly spending limits.
ww.A job title only, shown on a business ca: A job title shows position and can support formal authority, but power is the ability to influence behavior, which does not depend on a title alone.
ww.Electricity used to run machines in the: Electricity running machines is the physical meaning of power, not the organizational meaning, which refers to influence over people rather than energy supply.

rw: Legitimate power comes from a formal position in the organization, such as manager or supervisor, which gives the holder the recognized right to direct others.

ww.Power from charm and personal appeal: Power from charm and personal appeal is referent or charismatic power. Legitimate power comes from a formal position, not from being liked or admired.
ww.Power from rewards that managers give: Power from rewards is reward power. Legitimate power comes from holding a formal position, not from the ability to hand out rewards.
ww.Power from expertise and special skills: Power from expertise and special skills is expert power. Legitimate power is based on position, so skill does not create it.

rw: Expert power is influence based on specialized knowledge or skill, so people follow someone because they trust that person's competence in a field.

ww.Power from title or rank in the company': Power from title or rank is legitimate power. Expert power stems from knowledge and skill, not from the position held in the hierarchy.
ww.Power from punishment by taking away rew: Power from taking away rewards or punishing is coercive power, not expert power, which depends on skill and knowledge rather than threats.
ww.Power from charm and personal appeal wit: Power from charm and personal appeal is referent power. Expert power comes from specialized knowledge and skill, not from being liked.

rw: Referent power is influence based on admiration, respect and personal connection, so people follow a leader they identify with and want to be like.

ww.Power from force or the threat of punish: Power from force or the threat of punishment is coercive power. Referent power is about admiration and personal connection, not fear.
ww.Power from expertise and special skills: Power from expertise and special skills is expert power. Referent power comes from admiration and connection to a person, not from competence.
ww.Power from position or title in the orga: Power from position or title is legitimate power. Referent power is built on personal admiration, so it does not require any formal rank.

rw: Coercive power is influence based on the ability to punish, such as discipline, demotion or dismissal, so people comply because they fear negative consequences.

ww.Influence from expertise and special ski: Influence from expertise and skill is expert power. Coercive power rests on the ability to punish, not on knowledge.
ww.Influence from charm and personal appeal: Influence from charm and personal appeal is referent power. Coercive power depends on threats and punishment rather than on being liked.
ww.Influence from rewards given to workers: Influence from rewards is reward power, which is the opposite approach. Coercive power works through the threat of punishment and not through giving benefits.

rw: Reward power is influence based on the ability to give rewards such as raises, bonuses, promotions or praise, so people comply to gain those benefits.

ww.Influence from title or rank in the firm: Influence from title or rank is legitimate power. Reward power is based on the ability to give rewards, not on position alone.
ww.Influence from expertise gained by knowl: Influence from expertise gained through knowledge is expert power. Reward power depends on controlling things people value, such as raises, bonuses and praise.
ww.Influence from fear of being punished at: Influence from fear of being punished is coercive power, which is the opposite of reward power, since reward power uses benefits instead of threats.

rw: This feedback is specific, balanced and actionable. It notes a strength, then suggests adding data in section two, so the employee knows exactly how to improve the report.

ww.'Your report was bad, and you should hav: Calling a report bad and saying it should be better gives no specific detail about what to fix, so it is vague criticism, not constructive feedback.
ww.'Whatever, it's fine, I did not read it: Saying it is fine without reading the report gives no real feedback at all. It shows indifference and offers nothing the employee can use to improve.
ww.'You always mess up, and this latest rep: Saying someone always messes up and does not care is a personal attack with a sweeping judgment. It offers no specific improvement and will damage trust.

rw: A vision describes where an organization wants to go in the future, while a mission states why it exists and what it does today, so this contrast is accurate.

ww.A vision is the list of daily tasks whil: This swaps the two terms. Daily tasks are operations, not a vision, and the mission is not a ten-year future but the organization's present purpose.
ww.They are identical, because a vision and: The two statements differ. A vision looks ahead to a desired future, and a mission explains current purpose, so saying they are identical is incorrect.
ww.A mission is the future only, while a vi: This reverses the definitions. A vision is the future the organization aims for, and a mission is its purpose, not a statement of staff's daily work.

rw: Leaders shape culture through the values they model in their own behavior, the behaviors they reward, and what they communicate, because employees copy what leaders do.

ww.Through posters only that hang on the wa: Posters alone do not shape culture. Culture is built by what leaders actually do, reward and say, and wall hangings that conflict with behavior have little effect.
ww.By ignoring behavior and never rewarding: Ignoring behavior sends a message too, since people learn that anything goes. Leaders shape culture by acting on behavior with reward or correction, not by staying passive.
ww.By secret rules that only the top manage: Secret rules known only to top managers cannot guide behavior, because staff cannot follow what they do not know. Culture forms from visible, shared values and conduct.

rw: Change management is a structured approach for helping people and organizations adapt to change, using planning, communication and support so new methods are adopted smoothly.

ww.Making coins at the mint for use as mone: Making coins at a mint is a government function related to currency, not business. Change management concerns helping people and organizations adjust to new ways of working.
ww.Avoiding all change, so that the firm ke: Avoiding all change is the opposite of change management, which exists to plan and guide change so the organization can adapt, not to keep things the same.
ww.Changing management staff only so that n: Replacing managers is a staffing action, not change management. The field deals with how people and processes adapt to any change, not merely who holds the leadership posts.

rw: Fear of the unknown or of losing control is a common cause of resistance, because people worry about job security, new skills and changed routines.

ww.Too much communication tires the staff: Too much communication is rarely a cause of resistance. Resistance usually grows when communication is lacking, and tiredness from updates is not the typical reason people resist.
ww.Clear benefits shown to the staff: Clear benefits shown to staff reduce resistance rather than cause it, since people are more willing to accept a change when they see its value.
ww.Early involvement of all the staff: Early involvement reduces resistance by giving staff a voice and ownership, so it works against resistance and cannot be a common cause of it.

rw: Explaining the reasons and involving employees early builds understanding and ownership, which lowers fear and resistance, so it is the best action here.

ww.Announcing it suddenly with no warning t: Announcing a change suddenly gives people no time to adjust and increases fear and resistance, so surprise is likely to make the problem worse.
ww.Keeping it secret from employees until t: Keeping a change secret until the last day builds distrust and rumors, which raises resistance rather than reducing it.
ww.Forcing it without input from the staff: Forcing a change without staff input leaves affected employees feeling powerless, which fuels resistance, so it does not help the change succeed.

rw: Kotter's eight-step model begins with creating a sense of urgency, so people see why change is needed now and become motivated to act.

ww.Celebrate wins: Celebrating wins is a later step in Kotter's model, after short-term wins have been created. The model begins with building urgency instead.
ww.End the change: Ending the change is not a step in Kotter's model, which finishes with embedding the change in culture rather than stopping it.
ww.Anchor changes: Anchoring changes in the culture is the final step of Kotter's model, not the first. It comes only after the change has been built and shown to work.

rw: Tuckman's model describes the stages a team moves through as it develops, namely forming, storming, norming and performing, so this is the correct list.

ww.Planning, buying, selling and billing: Planning, buying, selling and billing are business transactions, not stages of how a team develops, so they do not describe Tuckman's model.
ww.Hiring, firing, paying and training: Hiring, firing, paying and training are human resource activities, not the group development stages that Tuckman identified.
ww.Start, stop, wait, go, and repeat: Start, stop, wait, go and repeat are not Tuckman's stages. His model names forming, storming, norming and performing as the sequence of team development.

rw: Storming is the stage where members assert their views and compete over roles and ideas, so conflict is typical at this stage of team development.

ww.Perfect harmony among members: Perfect harmony is not typical of storming. Harmony appears later, in norming and performing, once members have worked through differences.
ww.Introductions only as members meet: Introductions as members meet describe the forming stage, which comes before storming, when people are polite and still getting to know one another.
ww.Dissolution of the team soon: Dissolution comes at the adjourning stage, when the team ends. Storming happens early in development, when members are still working out how to cooperate.

rw: In norming, teams establish shared norms, resolve earlier conflicts, and begin to cooperate more, building trust and cohesion as members accept roles and ground rules.

ww.Disband and go their separate ways soon: Disbanding is the adjourning stage, at the end of the team's life. Norming happens earlier, after storming, when the team is still working together.
ww.Meet for the first time and learn names: Meeting for the first time and learning names is the forming stage, which comes before norming in the sequence of team development.
ww.Argue constantly about the roles and goa: Arguing constantly about roles and goals describes the storming stage, which precedes norming, where members start to settle those disagreements.

rw: In the performing stage the team works effectively toward its goals with high trust, clear roles and strong cooperation, which is why productivity is highest at this stage.

ww.Meet for the first time and agree on the: Meeting for the first time and agreeing on a plan describes forming, the first stage, which comes well before a team reaches performing.
ww.Fight over roles and fight over goals ag: Fighting over roles and goals describes storming, an earlier stage, whereas performing teams have already settled such issues and work smoothly.
ww.End the project and disband the group fo: Ending the project and disbanding the group is the adjourning stage, which follows performing rather than describing it.

rw: Groupthink is when a group values harmony over critical thinking, so members hide concerns and a risky plan goes ahead without proper challenge.

ww.Healthy debate: Healthy debate involves openly raising concerns and disagreement, but this team stays silent to keep harmony, so it is the opposite of healthy debate.
ww.Delegation: Delegation means assigning tasks to others. The team here suppresses concerns about a risky plan, which has nothing to do with handing off work.
ww.Benchmarking: Benchmarking is comparing performance with best practices. Staying quiet about a risky plan to keep harmony is a group decision flaw, not a comparison method.

rw: Encouraging dissent and inviting outside views brings in critical thinking and fresh information, which breaks the pressure for false harmony and prevents groupthink.

ww.Punish disagreement so members learn to: Punishing disagreement teaches members to stay quiet and obey, which is exactly what causes groupthink, so it makes the problem worse.
ww.Limit discussion to the leader's own ide: Limiting discussion to the leader's own ideas shuts out other perspectives and strengthens conformity, which increases the risk of groupthink instead of preventing it.
ww.Seek only agreement and avoid outside vi: Seeking only agreement and avoiding outside views is how groupthink develops, because the group never tests its plan against different opinions.

rw: Diversity in the workplace means differences among people in background, experience and perspective, such as age, gender, culture and skills, which can improve ideas.

ww.Everyone being alike in background, age: Everyone being alike in background, age and views is uniformity, the opposite of diversity, which means including real differences among people.
ww.Only one gender on the team, with the sa: Having only one gender in the same roles is a lack of diversity, so it contradicts the idea rather than defining it.
ww.Only one age group among the staff, all: One age group with the same views is uniform, not diverse. Diversity needs a mix of ages, backgrounds and perspectives among employees.

rw: Inclusion means creating an environment where all people feel valued, respected and able to participate fully, whatever their background, so their contributions are used.

ww.Hiring one person from a minority group: Hiring one person from a minority group for one post is tokenism. It does not create an environment where all people feel valued and able to participate.
ww.Counting employees by background and rec: Counting employees by background and reporting the numbers measures diversity but does not mean people feel valued, so it is a count, not inclusion.
ww.Excluding some people from the group so: Excluding some people is the opposite of inclusion. Inclusion means involving everyone, so leaving people out to make others comfortable defeats the purpose.

rw: CSR is a company's commitment to operate ethically and contribute to society, including care for employees, communities and the environment, beyond making a profit.

ww.Maximizing profit only and ignoring the: Maximizing profit only and ignoring people or the planet is the opposite of CSR, which asks companies to consider their social and environmental impact.
ww.Avoiding laws and rules that limit what: Avoiding laws and rules is unethical and often illegal, whereas CSR is a commitment to responsible behavior beyond simply following regulations.
ww.Reducing taxes only by moving profits to: Moving profits to low-tax places only to cut taxes is tax avoidance, which does not contribute to society, so it is not CSR.

rw: A code of conduct is a set of written guidelines on expected behavior within an organization, so employees know the standards for ethical and professional conduct.

ww.A secret code used by staff to send priv: A code of conduct is not a secret code for private messages. It is a public document that states expected behavior, not a way of hiding communication.
ww.A pay plan that sets the wages and bonus: A pay plan sets wages and bonuses and is a compensation document. A code of conduct sets behavior standards, so the two are unrelated.
ww.A product list that shows the goods that: A product list shows what the company makes and sells. A code of conduct covers how employees should behave, not what is sold.

rw: A whistleblower is a person who reports wrongdoing, such as fraud or safety violations, within or outside an organization, often to authorities or higher management.

ww.A sports referee only, who calls fouls i: A sports referee calls fouls in a match, which is a different role. A whistleblower reports misconduct inside an organization, and is not limited to sports.
ww.A manager who sets goals and assigns the: A manager who sets goals and assigns work is doing normal supervision, not whistleblowing, which means exposing wrongdoing instead of directing the work of staff.
ww.A rule breaker who is caught breaking th: A whistleblower is the person who reports a rule breaker, not the rule breaker. The role is to expose misconduct, not to commit it.

rw: An ethical dilemma is a situation where choosing among options involves conflicting moral values, so every choice has some ethical cost and no option is fully right.

ww.A scheduling issue in which two meetings: Two meetings booked at the same time is a scheduling conflict that can be solved with logistics. It does not involve conflicting moral values, so it is not an ethical dilemma.
ww.A clear rule to follow that tells staff: A clear rule telling staff exactly what to do removes the difficulty, whereas a dilemma arises when the right course is unclear and values conflict.
ww.A budget error in which the totals for c: A budget error where totals do not add up is an accounting mistake, which can be corrected, and it does not involve a moral choice.

rw: Reporting the overcharge through proper channels is honest, protects the company's money, and does not depend on the friendship, so it is the best ethical step.

ww.Retaliate against the supplier: Retaliating against the supplier is a hostile act that does not fix the overcharge and may be unethical or illegal, so it is not the best step.
ww.Ignore it and say nothing to anyone: Ignoring the overcharge lets the company lose money and puts personal loyalty above duty, which is an ethical failure by omission.
ww.Hide the invoice to keep the supplier: Hiding the invoice to protect the supplier is concealment that could count as fraud, and it harms the company, so it is clearly unethical.

rw: Selection is the process of choosing the best candidate from the applicant pool, using tools such as interviews, tests and reference checks to decide who gets the job.

ww.Attracting applicants through ads and jo: Attracting applicants through ads and job fairs is recruitment, which comes before selection. Selection starts once there is a pool of applicants to choose from.
ww.Terminating employees who break the rule: Terminating employees who break rules is discipline or dismissal, which happens after hiring, so it is not selection.
ww.Training new staff in the skills needed: Training new staff in the skills for the job is orientation and development, which comes after selection, once the person has been chosen.

rw: Internal recruitment rewards employees with promotion opportunities, which boosts morale, and it saves training time because the person already knows the firm.

ww.It brings brand new ideas from fresh eye: Bringing in brand new ideas from fresh eyes is a benefit of external recruitment, since internal candidates already know the organization and its current thinking.
ww.It is always slower and costs much more: Internal recruitment is not always slower or costlier. It usually saves time and money, so the claim that it is slower and more expensive is wrong.
ww.It costs more and takes longer than othe: Internal recruitment usually costs less and is faster than hiring outsiders, since it avoids ads and long orientation, so costing more and taking longer is wrong.

rw: External recruitment brings in new ideas, skills and experience from outside the organization, which can improve the firm and widen the pool of candidates.

ww.It rewards current staff with promotions: Rewarding current staff with promotions is an advantage of internal recruitment, not external recruitment, which looks outside the organization for candidates.
ww.It requires no screening of any applican: External recruitment still needs screening of applicants, since candidates are unknown, so saying no screening is required is wrong.
ww.It always costs less than internal hirin: External hiring often costs more because of ads and recruiters, so it does not always cost less than internal hiring.

rw: A behavioral interview question asks candidates to describe past actions in real situations, because past behavior is a good predictor of how someone will act in future.

ww.A yes/no question that can be answered w: A yes or no question gives little information about behavior. Behavioral questions ask for detailed stories, so a one-word answer does not fit them.
ww.A hypothetical riddle that tests how wel: A hypothetical riddle tests puzzle-solving rather than past behavior, and behavioral questions ask about real events the candidate has already experienced.
ww.A salary question about the pay that the: A salary question concerns the pay a candidate wants, which is about compensation, not about describing past actions, so it is not behavioral.

rw: "Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict" asks for a real past example, which is how behavioral questions are phrased and why they predict future behavior.

ww.'What would you do if...?' which asks ab: "What would you do if...?" is a hypothetical or situational question about an imaginary case. A behavioral question asks about something that really happened.
ww.'Are you a team player, and do you like: Asking if someone is a team player invites a simple yes or no. A behavioral question would ask for a specific example of teamwork in the past.
ww.'Where do you live, and how far is your: Where someone lives and how far the office is concerns logistics, not past behavior, so it is not behavioral and could raise fairness issues.

rw: Asking about plans to have children is generally illegal because it can lead to discrimination based on sex, family status or pregnancy, and it is unrelated to job ability.

ww.'Why do you want to join our firm?': Asking why someone wants to join the firm is a normal, lawful question about motivation and interest in the role, so it is allowed.
ww.'What are your strengths and skills?': Asking about strengths and skills is a standard job-related question that helps judge fit, so it is legal and appropriate.
ww.'Can you work some evenings a week?': Asking about availability for evenings is a lawful job-related question, as long as it is asked of all candidates and relates to the real schedule.

rw: A background check verifies a candidate's history, such as past employment, education and criminal record, to confirm the information given and reduce hiring risk.

ww.A skill test that checks how well a cand: A skill test checks how well a candidate can do job tasks, while a background check verifies a candidate's history, so these two are different.
ww.A review of a building to check its safe: Reviewing a building for safety and fire exits is a facility inspection, not a check on a candidate, so it is unrelated to a background check.
ww.A pay review in which the manager looks: A pay review looks at salaries to decide on raises, which concerns current employees, not the verification of a new candidate's history.

rw: An applicant tracking system is software that manages job applications and screens resumes, helping recruiters store, sort and follow candidates through the hiring process.

ww.A payroll system that pays the staff and: A payroll system pays staff and records hours, which is a different HR function. An ATS handles job applications during hiring, not salaries.
ww.A time clock that staff use to punch in: A time clock lets staff punch in and out of a shift, which tracks attendance. An ATS tracks applicants during recruitment instead.
ww.A chat tool that lets employees send qui: A chat tool for quick messages is a communication app. An ATS is hiring software that tracks applicants, so messaging is not its purpose.

rw: A fringe benefit is a non-wage reward, such as health insurance, retirement contributions or paid time off, that adds to total compensation beyond regular pay.

ww.A salary raise only, given to staff each: A salary raise only is a wage increase, which is direct pay. A fringe benefit is a non-wage reward, so it differs from salary.
ww.A fine charged to staff who break the ru: A fine charged for breaking rules is a penalty, which is the opposite of a reward, so it cannot be a fringe benefit.
ww.A penalty given to staff who arrive late: A penalty for lateness is a disciplinary action. Fringe benefits are extras that employees gain, not punishments given for poor conduct.

rw: Commission is 5% times $80,000, which is 0.05 x 80,000 = $4,000, so this is the correct amount for her commission.

ww.$400: $400 is only 0.5% of $80,000, which is a decimal slip. Five percent is 0.05, and 0.05 x 80,000 gives $4,000, not $400.
ww.$16,000: $16,000 would be 20% of $80,000, which is 0.20 x 80,000. The rate here is 5%, so 0.05 x 80,000 is $4,000, not $16,000.
ww.$80,005: $80,005 simply adds 5 to the sales figure, which misreads a percentage as a flat amount. Five percent of $80,000 is $4,000.

rw: A performance review is a periodic evaluation of an employee's performance, usually done yearly, that gives feedback, sets goals and informs pay and promotion decisions.

ww.A budget review of what the firm spent l: A budget review looks at the firm's spending, which is a finance matter. A performance review evaluates an individual employee's work.
ww.A sales report of what the firm sold ove: A sales report records what the firm sold, which is a business result. A performance review evaluates the work of an employee, so this is different.
ww.A review of a product by a customer who: A customer's review of a product is feedback on goods. A performance review is conducted by an employer to assess an employee, not a product.

rw: The halo effect is letting one positive trait influence the overall evaluation, so a person who excels at one thing is rated high in everything else.

ww.Using data only to rate each worker, wit: Using data only to rate workers is an objective method, not the halo effect, which is a bias caused by letting one impression color the rest.
ww.Rating everyone low because of one bad t: Rating everyone low because of one bad trait is the opposite bias, called the horn effect, since the halo effect works through a positive trait.
ww.Rating accurately across all traits for: Rating accurately across all traits for the whole period is good practice, not a bias, so it is the absence of the halo effect.

rw: The recency effect is overweighting recent events instead of the whole review period, so the last few weeks wrongly count more than the full year.

ww.Ignoring all events that happened in the: Ignoring all events from the review period would ignore evidence entirely, whereas the recency effect focuses too much on the latest events.
ww.Rating by tenure, so that longer-serving: Rating by tenure, where longer service gives the top score, is seniority bias, not recency bias, which is about the timing of events.
ww.Considering the whole year with each mon: Considering the whole year with each month weighted equally is the fair method that avoids recency bias, so it is the cure, not the effect.

rw: Job enlargement adds more tasks of a similar skill level to a job, which widens it horizontally and reduces monotony without raising authority.

ww.Reducing tasks to give workers less to d: Reducing tasks to give workers less to do is job reduction or simplification, not enlargement, which increases the number of tasks in a job.
ww.Adding higher authority such as power to: Adding higher authority such as the power to hire is job enrichment, which deepens the job vertically, so it differs from enlargement.
ww.Cutting hours to save pay costs for the: Cutting hours to save pay costs is a cost measure, not a redesign of job tasks, so it has nothing to do with enlargement.

rw: Job sharing is when two part-time employees split one full-time position, dividing the duties, hours and pay between them, which gives staff flexibility.

ww.One person holding two jobs with two dif: One person holding two jobs with different employers is dual employment, whereas job sharing splits one position between two people at one employer.
ww.Sharing salary with a boss who pays a cu: Sharing salary with a boss is not job sharing, which divides duties and pay of a single full-time position between two part-time employees.
ww.Sharing office space among workers who h: Sharing office space among workers is desk sharing or hot desking, which concerns space, not splitting a single job between people.

rw: Telecommuting is working from a remote location, such as home, using technology like the internet and phones to stay connected with the workplace.

ww.Working in a phone booth on a landline p: Working in a phone booth on a landline is not telecommuting, which relies on modern technology to do office work from a remote place.
ww.Selling phones and phone plans to custom: Selling phones and plans is a retail job, not telecommuting. The word means working remotely using technology, whatever the occupation.
ww.Commuting by train to the main office ea: Commuting by train means traveling to the office, which is the opposite of telecommuting, where the worker avoids the daily trip by working remotely.

rw: A collective bargaining agreement is a contract negotiated between an employer and a union covering pay, hours and working conditions for the represented employees.

ww.A sales contract in which a buyer agrees: A bulk purchase contract is a sales agreement between buyer and seller. A collective bargaining agreement is negotiated between employers and a union on work terms.
ww.A lease in which a company rents office: A lease for office space is a property contract between a company and a landlord, not an agreement about pay and conditions for union members.
ww.A personal loan that an employee takes f: A personal loan from a credit union is a financial contract for one employee. A collective bargaining agreement covers groups of workers through their union.

rw: A labor union is an organization of workers that bargains with employers for better pay, hours and working conditions, giving employees a collective voice.

ww.A government agency that makes laws abou: A government agency that makes labor laws is a regulator. A labor union is an organization of workers, not a government body.
ww.A customer club that gives discounts and: A customer club gives discounts to loyal shoppers, which is a marketing program. A labor union represents workers, not customers.
ww.A company owner group that meets to vote: A group of owners voting on strategy is a board or shareholder body. A union is made up of workers, not owners.

rw: A grievance procedure is a formal process for employees to raise and resolve complaints about treatment or conditions, ensuring issues are heard and addressed fairly.

ww.A pay system that sets the wages and bon: A pay system that sets wages and bonuses is a compensation structure. A grievance procedure handles complaints, so it has no role in setting pay.
ww.A way to fire workers who break the rule: A series of steps to fire workers who break rules is a disciplinary process. A grievance procedure instead lets employees raise their own complaints.
ww.A hiring process in which candidates app: A hiring process in which candidates apply and interview is recruitment and selection, which has nothing to do with handling employee complaints.

rw: Downsizing is reducing the workforce to cut costs, often through layoffs or early retirements, in order to make the organization leaner or more profitable.

ww.Hiring more staff to raise output: Hiring more staff to raise output is expansion, which is the opposite of downsizing, as downsizing reduces the number of employees.
ww.Opening new branches in the market: Opening new branches is growth in locations and often adds staff, which is the opposite of downsizing, which shrinks the organization.
ww.Raising salaries for all workers: Raising salaries for all workers increases costs, whereas downsizing aims to cut costs by reducing the number of employees.

rw: Outsourcing means contracting work to an outside company instead of doing it in-house, often to cut costs or use specialist skills.

ww.Hiring interns for the summer months: Hiring summer interns adds temporary staff to the firm's own payroll, so it is not outsourcing, which uses an outside company to do work.
ww.Moving offices to a new building or city: Moving offices changes location, not who does the work. Outsourcing means giving tasks to an outside company, not moving to a new place.
ww.Doing all work in-house, no outside help: Doing all work in-house with no outside help is the opposite of outsourcing, which relies on external firms for some tasks.

rw: An employee assistance program is a confidential service offering counseling and support to employees for personal or work-related issues such as stress, family, health or substance problems.

ww.A sales program that trains staff to clo: A sales program that trains staff to close deals is sales training. An EAP offers confidential support for personal and work problems.
ww.A training schedule that lists the dates: A training schedule lists course dates for staff. An EAP is a support service that gives counseling, so a schedule does not match.
ww.A pay plan that sets how much money each: A pay plan sets how much each employee earns. An EAP is a confidential support service, not a compensation structure.

rw: A probationary period lets the employer evaluate a new hire's fit and performance before granting permanent status, and lets the employee judge the job too.

ww.To delay pay for new hires until they ha: A probationary period does not delay pay for a year. New hires are paid from the start, while the period usually lasts only a few months.
ww.To end the job of a new hire after the f: Ending a new hire's job after the first week without notice is not the purpose. The period is for fair evaluation, not instant dismissal.
ww.To punish new hires who make a mistake b: The period is not meant to punish mistakes by cutting pay. It exists to assess fit and performance, with support, not to reduce wages.

rw: Employee engagement is the level of commitment and enthusiasm that employees have for their work and organization, which drives productivity, retention and quality.

ww.A work schedule that lists each employee: A work schedule lists start and end times and is a scheduling tool. Engagement refers to commitment and enthusiasm, not hours of work.
ww.A promise that is made before a wedding: A promise before a wedding is the social meaning of the word engagement. In business, employee engagement means commitment to work, not a marriage promise.
ww.A pay level that rises each year an empl: A pay level that rises with years of service is a seniority-based pay scale, whereas engagement is about commitment and enthusiasm, not wages.

rw: The first step is to identify and define the problem, because a solution cannot be chosen until the real problem is clearly understood.

ww.Evaluate all of the results: Evaluating results comes last in problem solving, after a solution has been carried out, so it cannot be the first step.
ww.Implement a solution at once: Implementing a solution at once skips defining the problem and weighing options, which risks wasting effort on the wrong issue, so it is not first.
ww.Choose a solution right away: Choosing a solution right away skips defining the problem and gathering information, so the choice may be poor. This step comes after analysis.

rw: After defining the problem, you gather information and identify causes, so that the later solution addresses the real source of the problem.

ww.Implement the chosen solution now: Implementing the solution comes later, after the causes are known and options are weighed. Doing it right after defining the problem skips analysis.
ww.Evaluate results before gathering facts: Evaluating results before gathering facts is out of order, because results appear only after a solution is implemented, not directly after problem definition.
ww.Celebrate the success with the whole tea: Celebrating success is a final step, if at all, and cannot come right after defining a problem that has not been solved yet.

rw: A fishbone or Ishikawa diagram identifies possible causes of a problem by category, such as people, methods, machines and materials, helping teams find root causes.

ww.Scheduling shifts for workers on the sho: Scheduling shifts is done with rosters or scheduling software. A fishbone diagram is a cause analysis tool, so it does not plan work hours.
ww.Budgeting for the costs of a project ove: Budgeting for a project's costs uses financial planning tools, not a fishbone diagram, which maps out possible causes of a problem.
ww.Tracking sales of each product in each s: Tracking sales by product and store uses reports or charts of sales data. A fishbone diagram looks at causes, not sales figures.

rw: A Pareto chart is based on the 80/20 principle, which says that a few causes produce most of the effects, so effort goes to the vital few.

ww.Equal causes, where every cause produces: Pareto charts do not assume equal causes. They show that causes differ greatly in effect, with a few causes being much larger than the rest.
ww.Random causes, where effects have no pat: Effects of causes are not random, since a Pareto chart reveals a clear pattern in which a few causes dominate, so random is wrong.
ww.One cause always, as every problem has a: Pareto analysis rests on the fact that problems have many causes and a few matter most, so the claim of a single cause is incorrect.

rw: The Pareto principle states that roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes, which matches 80% of complaints coming from 20% of product types.

ww.Benchmarking rivals: Benchmarking compares your practices with rivals or leaders. It does not explain why 20% of products cause 80% of complaints.
ww.Groupthink in a team: Groupthink is a team decision flaw caused by pressure to agree. It has nothing to do with the distribution of complaints among products.
ww.Delegation of tasks: Delegation means handing tasks to others. It is not a principle for analyzing how complaints are concentrated in a small share of products.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up when making a choice, so it measures what you lose by choosing one option over another.

ww.The price paid for goods and services in: The price paid for goods is simply the money cost, not the opportunity cost, which measures the value of what you give up by choosing.
ww.The interest cost on a loan over the len: Interest on a loan is a financing cost, not opportunity cost, which is about alternatives forgone, not about the charge for borrowing money.
ww.A tax paid on the sale of a good or serv: A tax on the sale of a good is a government charge, not opportunity cost, which concerns the next best use of resources that you give up.

rw: A bias in thinking is a systematic tendency that skews judgment, causing people to favor certain ideas or conclusions without good reason.

ww.A neutral view of all sides and the fact: A neutral view of all sides and facts is objectivity, which is the opposite of bias, since bias distorts how we see information.
ww.A formula used to compute costs and sale: A formula used to compute costs and sales is a calculation tool. A bias in thinking is a mental tendency, not a formula.
ww.A fact that anyone can verify by checkin: A fact that anyone can verify is objective information, whereas a bias is a leaning that distorts judgment and is not verifiable fact.

rw: Confirmation bias is seeking only information that supports what you already believe, which matches the manager reading only reports backing her preferred plan.

ww.Objective thinking: Objective thinking weighs all evidence fairly. A manager reading only reports that support her plan is selective, so this is not objective.
ww.Critical thinking: Critical thinking examines evidence from all sides. Reading only supportive reports avoids challenge, so it is the opposite of critical thinking.
ww.Delegation of work: Delegation means assigning work to others. The manager's selective reading of reports is a thinking bias, not a way of sharing tasks.

rw: Anchoring bias is relying too heavily on the first piece of information encountered, such as an initial price, when making later judgments and decisions.

ww.Using many sources to check the facts fr: Using many sources to check facts from different views is good practice that reduces bias, so it is the opposite of anchoring.
ww.Sailing a boat on open water, where the: Sailing and anchoring a boat is the physical meaning of the word. Anchoring bias is a mental habit of fixating on first information.
ww.Ignoring all numbers and data that are g: Ignoring numbers and data given at the start is the reverse of anchoring bias, in which the first information has too much influence.

rw: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing a course because of past investment instead of future value, ignoring that money already spent cannot be recovered.

ww.Budgeting carefully so that future costs: Budgeting so that only future costs count is the correct way to avoid the fallacy, so it describes sound reasoning, not the fallacy.
ww.Cutting losses early once it is clear th: Cutting losses early once a project is clearly failing is rational and is the opposite of the sunk cost fallacy.
ww.Ignoring all costs, whether they were pa: Ignoring all costs, past or future, would be careless. The fallacy is specifically letting past costs drive decisions, not ignoring every cost.

rw: Continuing to fund a failing project because $2 million was already spent is the sunk cost fallacy, since that money is gone whatever happens next.

ww.Opportunity cost thinking: Opportunity cost thinking compares the value of the best alternative forgone. Funding a failing project because of past spending is not that kind of reasoning.
ww.Benchmarking firms: Benchmarking compares performance against other firms. It does not explain why a company keeps funding a failing project because of money already spent.
ww.Sound investing rules: Sound investing looks at future returns, not past spending. Throwing more money at a failing project because of $2 million spent is poor reasoning.

rw: An ad hominem attack targets the person making the argument rather than the argument itself, which is a fallacy because it avoids the real issue.

ww.Addressing the argument with facts and r: Addressing the argument with facts and reasons is a valid response, whereas an ad hominem attack targets the person instead of the argument.
ww.Asking a question about the facts of the: Asking a question about the facts is a legitimate way to test an argument, not an attack on the person who made it.
ww.Citing evidence to support the points in: Citing evidence to support the points in an argument is proper reasoning, so it is not an ad hominem attack.

rw: A false dilemma presents only two options when more exist, wrongly forcing a choice and hiding other possible solutions or middle ground.

ww.Listing facts to support the whole argum: Listing facts to support an argument is sound reasoning and not a false dilemma, which wrongly limits the choices available.
ww.Asking for ideas from the whole team fir: Asking the team for ideas first is a way to widen options, so it is the opposite of a false dilemma.
ww.Offering many options so the person can: Offering many options lets the person choose freely, so it is the reverse of a false dilemma, which limits choices artificially.

rw: The slippery slope fallacy claims that one step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without proof, assuming a chain of events that has not been shown.

ww.A budget rule that limits how much each: A budget rule that limits department spending is a financial control. The slippery slope fallacy is a flaw in reasoning, not a spending policy.
ww.A proven chain of events in which each s: A proven chain of events in which each step causes the next is valid reasoning. A slippery slope is the claim made without proof.
ww.A skiing term for a steep hill that skie: A steep ski hill is the literal meaning of the words. The slippery slope fallacy is an argument error, not a feature of winter sports.

rw: A fact can be verified with evidence, while an opinion is a personal view or judgment that may differ between people, which is the key difference.

ww.They are identical, as both can be prove: Facts and opinions are not identical. A fact can be proven with evidence, while an opinion is a personal belief that cannot be proven in that way.
ww.A fact is a feeling that a person has ab: A fact is not a feeling. Feelings are subjective, whereas a fact is something that can be checked and shown to be true.
ww.An opinion can be proved, while a fact i: This reverses the terms. Facts, not opinions, can be proved, and opinions are views, so the statement mixes up the two ideas.

rw: Revenue grew 8% last year according to its report is a specific claim that can be checked against the report, so it is a verifiable fact.

ww.Our product is the best ever made and ev: Saying the product is the best ever made and every buyer agrees is a subjective claim with an absolute that cannot be verified, so it is opinion.
ww.That design is ugly and poorly made in t: Calling a design ugly and poorly made is a matter of taste and judgment, not a measurable claim, so it is an opinion.
ww.Employees love working here and are happ: Saying employees love working here and are happy with everything is a broad, subjective generalization that cannot be verified as stated, so it is opinion.

rw: Checking the author's expertise, evidence and potential bias is the standard way to judge credibility, since it tests who wrote it and why.

ww.Choose the first result shown by the sea: The first search result is not always the most credible, since ranking reflects popularity or advertising and not accuracy, so choosing it blindly is unreliable.
ww.Trust anything online since all posts on: Not everything online is checked. Many posts have no review process, so trusting anything on the web leads to misinformation.
ww.Prefer the loudest voice, as the most co: Confidence or loudness is not evidence. A confident speaker may still be wrong, so preferring the loudest voice does not test credibility.

rw: A primary source is an original firsthand account or data, such as a diary, interview, photograph or raw survey results.

ww.A summary of other works by a historian: A summary of other works by a historian is a secondary source, since it interprets earlier material rather than being firsthand.
ww.A textbook that reviews other works: A textbook that reviews other works is a secondary or tertiary source, because it summarizes research by others instead of presenting original evidence.
ww.A commentary on other written works: A commentary on other written works analyzes existing texts, so it is secondary, whereas primary sources are the original materials themselves.

rw: A hypothesis is a testable prediction or explanation that can be checked through experiments or observation, which is why it forms the starting point of research.

ww.A proven fact backed by lots of data: A proven fact backed by lots of data is an established finding, whereas a hypothesis is a proposal that still needs to be tested.
ww.A final conclusion after the experiment: A final conclusion after the experiment is the result, and a hypothesis comes before the experiment as the idea being tested.
ww.A random guess made with no real basis: A hypothesis is not a random guess with no basis. It is an informed, testable statement, usually based on observation or prior knowledge.

rw: Lateral thinking solves problems with creative approaches rather than step-by-step logic, looking at an issue from unexpected angles to find new ideas.

ww.Thinking sideways physically, by moving: Moving sideways physically is a bodily action, but lateral thinking is a mental approach that looks at problems from new angles.
ww.Avoiding change and sticking to the same: Avoiding change and sticking to routine is the opposite of lateral thinking, which seeks new, creative ways to approach a problem.
ww.Following strict steps in a fixed order: Following strict steps in a fixed order to reach one answer is linear or vertical thinking, which lateral thinking deliberately departs from.

rw: Design thinking is a human-centered approach to innovation that follows empathize, define, ideate, prototype and test, so solutions fit real user needs.

ww.A cost-cutting plan that lowers expenses: A cost-cutting plan trims budgets to lower expenses, which is a financial approach. Design thinking is a human-centered method for innovation.
ww.Drawing logos only, to create the visual: Drawing logos only covers visual branding. Design thinking is a wider problem-solving process that starts with understanding user needs.
ww.A hiring method that sorts applicants by: A hiring method that ranks applicants by test scores is a selection tool. Design thinking is a problem-solving process, not a recruiting system.

rw: A prototype is an early model of a product used to test ideas and gather feedback before final production, which saves time and cost.

ww.A budget of the costs and income that a: A budget of expected costs and income is a financial plan, not a model of a product, which is what a prototype is.
ww.A sales report of the units sold by the: A sales report lists units sold, which is a record of past results. A prototype is a draft version of a product made for testing.
ww.The final product that is sold to custom: The final product sold to customers is the finished item, whereas a prototype is an early version made for testing before release.

rw: A risk assessment identifies potential risks and judges their likelihood and impact, so managers can decide which ones to reduce, transfer or accept.

ww.Counting profits made by the firm in eac: Counting profits each quarter is accounting and reporting. A risk assessment looks forward at potential problems, not at income already earned.
ww.Ignoring risks and hoping that nothing w: Ignoring risks and hoping nothing goes wrong is the opposite of risk assessment, which is a deliberate review of what could go wrong.
ww.Buying insurance only, without looking a: Buying insurance only, without studying risk, skips the assessment. Insurance can be a response, but assessment first looks at the cause and size of risks.

rw: A risk matrix is a grid rating risks by likelihood and severity, which helps teams see which risks need action first.

ww.A budget of expected income and costs fo: A budget of income and costs is a financial plan. A risk matrix instead rates risks by how likely and how serious they are.
ww.A sales chart showing units sold in each: A sales chart showing units per region records sales results. A risk matrix is a grid that ranks risks, not a sales report.
ww.A list of employees and their jobs in th: A list of employees and their jobs is an organizational chart or staff list, not a tool for rating risks.

rw: Customer lifetime value is the total revenue a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship, which guides how much to spend on getting and keeping customers.

ww.A discount that a store gives to loyal c: A discount given to loyal customers is a loyalty reward. Customer lifetime value measures total revenue from a customer over time, not a price cut.
ww.A single sale that a customer makes the: A single first-visit sale is only one transaction. Lifetime value counts all the revenue a customer brings over the whole relationship, so one sale is not enough.
ww.A refund amount that a company returns w: A refund returned when a product is sent back is money leaving the company, whereas lifetime value counts the revenue a customer brings in.

rw: Retaining customers is cheaper because acquiring new ones requires marketing and sales costs, while existing customers already know the brand and need less persuasion.

ww.Existing customers cost nothing to keep,: Existing customers are not free to keep, since they still need service, communication and some marketing. They simply cost less than winning new ones.
ww.New customers are free to win, as they j: New customers are not free to win. Finding and persuading them takes marketing, sales time and money, which is why acquisition costs more.
ww.Marketing is free for most firms, so win: Marketing is not free for most firms, because advertising, staff and campaigns cost money. Winning new customers therefore has real costs, so this reasoning fails.

rw: A supplier relationship is a partnership between a business and the firms that provide its goods or services, built on trust, reliability and shared benefit.

ww.A customer complaint that is sent to the: A customer complaint is feedback about a product or service, not a relationship with suppliers, who provide goods to the business.
ww.A competitor rivalry between two firms t: A rivalry between competitors is competition for the same buyers, not a supplier relationship, which is based on cooperation and trade.
ww.An employee contract that sets the pay a: An employee contract sets pay and duties for a worker, which is an employment relationship and not a link with outside suppliers.

rw: A service-level agreement is a contract that defines the level of service a provider must deliver, such as response times and uptime, with remedies if it is missed.

ww.A hiring document that lists the duties: A hiring document listing duties and pay for a position is a job description or offer. An SLA is a contract that defines service levels.
ww.A tax form that firms file each year to: A tax form reports profits to the government and has nothing to do with service quality, which an SLA defines between provider and customer.
ww.A pay stub that shows the wages paid to: A pay stub shows wages paid in one period. An SLA is a service contract between a provider and a client, so the two are unrelated.

rw: BATNA stands for Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement, which is your best option if the negotiation fails and no deal is reached.

ww.Best attitude toward all of the parties: BATNA does not stand for best attitude toward all parties. It names the fallback option you have if talks fail, not a mindset.
ww.Budget and tax notice for the full year: A budget and tax notice for the year is an accounting item. BATNA is a negotiation term that has nothing to do with taxes.
ww.Basic agreement to nothing as both sides: Basic agreement to nothing as both sides quit is not what BATNA means. The N stands for negotiated, and the acronym refers to the best alternative.

rw: A strong BATNA increases bargaining power because you have a good alternative and need not accept a poor deal, so you can negotiate from strength.

ww.It weakens your bargaining power: A strong BATNA strengthens your position because you can walk away, so saying it weakens your bargaining power gets the effect backwards.
ww.It forces agreement from them: A strong BATNA gives you leverage but does not force the other side to agree, since they remain free to refuse.
ww.It has no effect on the talks: BATNA clearly matters. A good alternative changes how much you can demand and when you can walk away, so saying it has no effect is false.

rw: An elevator pitch is a brief persuasive summary of who you are or what you offer, short enough to deliver in about thirty seconds to a minute.

ww.A written contract that binds both sides: A written contract that binds both sides is a legal agreement. An elevator pitch is a short spoken summary, not a binding document.
ww.A long speech given at a conference to a: A long conference speech takes much more time than an elevator pitch, which is meant to be short enough to give during an elevator ride.
ww.A sales report that shows how many items: A sales report shows past sales figures. An elevator pitch is a short persuasive talk, not a report of items sold.

rw: Business etiquette is the accepted standards of professional behavior, such as politeness, punctuality and respectful communication, which help build good working relationships.

ww.Business law and the rules of contracts: Business law and contract rules are legal topics that bind parties. Etiquette covers social behavior and manners rather than legal rules.
ww.Accounting rules for the books of a firm: Accounting rules govern how a firm keeps its books. Etiquette concerns professional manners and conduct, so it is a different subject.
ww.Tax policy set by the government each ye: Tax policy is set by the government as a matter of public finance. Business etiquette instead refers to professional behavior norms among people at work.
